title: Photosynthesis
blurb: Write the photosynthesis equation, contrast the light-dependent reactions with the Calvin cycle by location, inputs and outputs, and explain where the oxygen comes from.
question: A houseplant on a sunny windowsill takes in carbon dioxide and gives off oxygen. In which part of the chloroplast is the oxygen released, which molecule does that oxygen come from, and how does the plant turn carbon dioxide into sugar?

teach.body: Formal definition: photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose: 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + light energy to C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂. It takes place in the chloroplasts of plants and algae (and in cyanobacteria, which have no chloroplasts). Plain English: plants are autotrophs, the producers of food chains. They catch sunlight, pull CO₂ from the air and water from the soil, and build sugar, releasing oxygen as a by-product.

teach.caption: Photosynthesis runs inside the chloroplasts. Note that the same cell also has mitochondria: plants respire too.

steps.label: Light reactions
steps.sub: Thylakoids: light absorbed, water split, O₂ out

steps.label: ATP + NADPH
steps.sub: Energy carriers pass to the stroma

steps.label: Calvin cycle
steps.sub: Stroma: CO₂ fixed into sugar (G3P to glucose)

teach.caption: ADP and NADP+ return from the Calvin cycle to the thylakoids to be recharged.

teach.body: Chlorophyll in the thylakoid membranes absorbs light, which excites electrons. To replace them, water is split (photolysis) into oxygen, H+ ions and electrons. The O₂ is released through the stomata. The energy of the excited electrons is used to make ATP and NADPH. Key point: the oxygen given off by a plant comes from WATER, not from carbon dioxide.

The light-independent reactions, or Calvin cycle, run in the stroma, the fluid around the thylakoids. They spend the ATP and NADPH from the light reactions to fix CO₂ into a three-carbon sugar (G3P), which is used to build glucose. Older texts call them the "dark reactions", but they do not need darkness: they normally run in daylight, because they depend on a steady supply of ATP and NADPH.

teach.caption: Leaves look green because chlorophyll reflects green light. Accessory pigments (carotenoids) capture some other wavelengths.

head: Substance
Route
Role
rows: Split for electrons; source of O₂
teach.caption: Stomata are leaf pores opened and closed by guard cells. Rate depends on light intensity, CO₂ level, temperature (enzymes) and water.
The overall equations are roughly the reverse of each other. Plants do both: photosynthesis in light, respiration all the time.

teach.body: Elena, a nursing applicant, grows basil under lights. In the thylakoids, chlorophyll absorbs the red and blue light, water is split and O₂ escapes through the stomata, while ATP and NADPH are made. In the stroma, the Calvin cycle uses them to fix CO₂ into sugar. When she raises the light and growth stops increasing, light is no longer the limit; adding CO₂ or keeping the plant watered and warm can raise the rate further. Switching to green bulbs would slow it, because green light is mostly reflected.

teach.text: Exam traps: photosynthesis USES CO₂ and RELEASES O₂; the O₂ comes from WATER, not CO₂; light reactions are in the THYLAKOIDS, the Calvin cycle in the STROMA; chlorophyll REFLECTS green; the "dark reactions" do not need darkness; chloroplast is the organelle, chlorophyll the pigment; plants also respire.

items: 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + light to C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂, in chloroplasts.
Light reactions (thylakoids): light absorbed, water split, O₂ released, ATP and NADPH made.
Calvin cycle (stroma): ATP and NADPH used to fix CO₂ into sugar.
O₂ released comes from water. CO₂ enters and O₂ leaves through stomata.
Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue, reflects green.
Rate depends on light, CO₂, temperature and water.

summary: You can now write the photosynthesis equation and contrast the light-dependent reactions (thylakoids: water split, O₂, ATP, NADPH) with the Calvin cycle (stroma: CO₂ fixed into sugar). You can also explain why leaves are green, where the released oxygen comes from, what limits the rate and how photosynthesis mirrors respiration.

A.q: Where in the chloroplast do the light-dependent reactions take place?
A.why: Chlorophyll and the light-reaction machinery sit in the thylakoid membranes.

whyNot.1: The stroma is the site of the Calvin cycle.
whyNot.2: The mitochondrial matrix hosts the Krebs cycle of respiration.
whyNot.3: The inner mitochondrial membrane holds the electron transport chain of respiration.

A.q: Which molecule is fixed into sugar during the Calvin cycle?
A.why: The Calvin cycle uses ATP and NADPH to fix carbon from CO₂ into sugar.

whyNot.0: Oxygen is released by the light reactions; it is not fixed.
whyNot.2: Water is split in the light reactions, not fixed into sugar.
whyNot.3: Chlorophyll absorbs light; it is a pigment, not a raw material.

A.q: Why do most plant leaves appear green?
options: Chloroplasts absorb red and green light.
Chlorophyll reflects red and blue light.
A.why: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light and reflects green, so leaves look green.

whyNot.0: Absorbed light is not seen; green is the light chlorophyll does NOT absorb.
whyNot.1: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light; green is reflected.
whyNot.2: Red and blue light are absorbed for photosynthesis, not reflected.

B.q: The oxygen gas released by a plant during photosynthesis comes from:
options: The Calvin cycle in the stroma
B.why: In the light-dependent reactions, water is split in the thylakoids and its oxygen is released as O₂.

whyNot.0: CO₂ is fixed into sugar in the Calvin cycle; it is not the source of the O₂ released.
whyNot.1: Glucose is a product of photosynthesis, not something broken down to release O₂.
whyNot.3: The Calvin cycle fixes CO₂ into sugar; it does not release oxygen.

B.q: Which statement about the Calvin cycle is accurate?
options: It runs in darkness and stops in light.
It splits water and releases oxygen.
It runs in the thylakoid membranes.
It uses ATP and NADPH to make sugar.
B.why: The Calvin cycle runs in the stroma and spends the ATP and NADPH from the light reactions to fix CO₂ into sugar.

whyNot.0: It does not need darkness; it runs in daylight, fed by the light reactions.
whyNot.1: Splitting water and releasing O₂ is the work of the light reactions.
whyNot.2: The thylakoid membranes host the light reactions; the Calvin cycle is in the stroma.

B.q: Which cells open and close the stomata that let CO₂ into a leaf?
B.why: Each stoma is a pore bordered by two guard cells, which open and close it.

whyNot.1: Root hairs absorb water and minerals from the soil.
whyNot.2: Xylem carries water up from the roots.
whyNot.3: Red blood cells are animal cells that carry oxygen in blood.

C.q: Which statement comparing photosynthesis and cellular respiration is accurate?
options: Respiration releases O₂ and uses CO₂.
Plant cells carry out both processes.
Animal cells carry out both processes.
C.why: Plant cells photosynthesize in chloroplasts and also carry out cellular respiration in their mitochondria.

whyNot.0: This is reversed: respiration uses O₂ and releases CO₂.
whyNot.1: Photosynthesis happens in chloroplasts; mitochondria carry out respiration.
whyNot.3: Animal cells have no chloroplasts, so they cannot photosynthesize.

C.q: A healthy plant sits in a sealed jar under bright light all day. What most likely happens to the CO₂ level in the jar?
options: It rises, as photosynthesis releases CO₂.
It falls, as photosynthesis outpaces respiration.
It rises, as plants respire but do not photosynthesize.
It stays the same, as plants do not exchange CO₂.
C.why: In bright light, photosynthesis uses CO₂ faster than the plant's respiration releases it, so the CO₂ level falls.

whyNot.0: Photosynthesis uses CO₂; it does not release it.
whyNot.2: Plants do both, and in bright light photosynthesis is the faster process.
whyNot.3: Plants take in CO₂ for photosynthesis and release it in respiration.

C.q: To make one molecule of glucose, how many molecules of CO₂ and of water does photosynthesis use?
C.why: 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + light energy gives C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂: six carbons in glucose need six CO₂.

whyNot.1: Glucose has six carbons, so one CO₂ cannot supply them.
whyNot.2: O₂ is a product of photosynthesis, not a reactant.
whyNot.3: Twelve CO₂ would supply twelve carbons, enough for two glucose molecules.

reteach.title: A solar-powered bakery
reteach.question: Imagine a bakery whose rooftop solar panels charge batteries that run the ovens. How does that bakery work like a chloroplast?

blocks.body: The rooftop panels (thylakoids) catch sunlight and charge batteries (ATP and NADPH). To work, the panels must split water, and the leftover oxygen drifts out the vents (stomata). Downstairs, the kitchen (stroma) uses the charged batteries to turn flour delivered from outside (CO₂) into bread (sugar), sending flat batteries (ADP, NADP+) back upstairs. The kitchen does not need the sun shining in; it needs charged batteries, which is why it works during the day.

blocks.text: The oxygen out the vents comes from the water split upstairs, not from the flour (CO₂) used in the kitchen.

explain.body: 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + light energy to C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂. Light energy becomes chemical energy stored in glucose, in the chloroplasts of plants and algae.

test.q: What are the products of photosynthesis?
test.why: Photosynthesis produces glucose and releases oxygen.

whyNot.0: CO₂ and water are the reactants of photosynthesis.
whyNot.1: CO₂ is used, not produced, by photosynthesis.
whyNot.2: Water is used, not produced, in the overall equation.

explain.body: In the thylakoid membranes, chlorophyll absorbs light, water is split, O₂ is released and the energy is stored in ATP and NADPH.

test.q: Which event happens in the light-dependent reactions?
options: Water is split and O₂ is released.
test.why: Light energy drives the splitting of water in the thylakoids, releasing O₂ and producing ATP and NADPH.

whyNot.0: Fixing CO₂ into sugar is the Calvin cycle in the stroma.
whyNot.2: Breaking glucose into pyruvate is glycolysis, part of respiration.
whyNot.3: Building glucose from G3P follows the Calvin cycle, not the light reactions.

explain.body: In the stroma, the cycle spends ATP and NADPH to fix CO₂ into G3P, which is used to make glucose. It is "light-independent" but runs in daylight, when the light reactions keep it supplied.

test.q: What does the Calvin cycle use to build sugar?
test.why: The Calvin cycle fixes CO₂ using the energy and electrons of ATP and NADPH from the light reactions.

whyNot.0: Water, light and chlorophyll are used in the light reactions.
whyNot.1: Glucose is the product, and O₂ is released elsewhere, not used.
whyNot.3: NADH is a carrier in respiration; the Calvin cycle uses NADPH and CO₂, not O₂.

explain.body: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light and reflects green. CO₂ enters and O₂ leaves through stomata, controlled by guard cells. The rate depends on light, CO₂, temperature and water.

test.q: On a sunny day, which change would most likely slow photosynthesis in a healthy plant?
options: Raising the CO₂ level in the air
Closing the stomata on the leaves
Watering the soil around the roots
Adding more red and blue light
test.why: Closed stomata stop CO₂ from entering the leaf, so the Calvin cycle runs short of carbon.

whyNot.0: More CO₂ supplies the Calvin cycle and tends to raise the rate.
whyNot.2: Water is a raw material; watering supports photosynthesis.
whyNot.3: Red and blue light are the wavelengths chlorophyll absorbs best.
